div.p: In applications ranging from uideo reception to telecommunications and packet conr7nunication to aircruft control, tasks enter periorlicdly and hove fixed response time constraints, but missing n deadline is acceptable, provided most deadlines are met. W e call such tasks "occasionally skippable". We look at the problem of uniprocessor scheduling of occasionnlly skippable periodic tusks in a n environment having periodic tasks. W e show that making optimal use of skips is NP-hard. W e then look at two algorithms called Skip-Over Algorithms (one a variant of earliest dendline first and one of rate monoton.ic scheduling) that exploit skips. We give schedulablli t y bounds for both.

A blue task instance may complete by its deadline or miss its deadline. When a task misses its deadline we say that the task (or deadline) instance was skipped. We characterize the possible skips of a task by its skip paramrter, 2 5 s 5 03, which gives the tolerance of this task to missing deadlines. The distance between two consecutive skips must, be at least s periods. That is, after missing a deadline at least s-1 task instances must meet their deadlines. The fact that s 2 2 implies that. if a blue task instance missed its deadline then the next occurrence of the same task must be red. When s = oci no skips are allowed. One can view the skip paramder as a Quality of Service (QOS) metric. (The higher s , the better the quality of service.

div.head: Examples to Train Your Intuition 1 Introduction
Basic Assumptions and Definitions
div.p: We consider a uni-processor syst,em in which preemption is possible at any time and costs nothing. All tasks are periodic but, they may ent,er the syst,em at any time. A task is characterized by its comput,ation requirements and period; t8he deadline of a t,ask equals its period. Tasks are assumed tlo be independent,, i.e., there are no precedence constraint,s among different tasks. A task t is divided into inst.ances where each instance occurs during a single period of the task. Every instance of a task can be red or blue. A red task instance must complete before its clpadline; a blue task instance can be aborted at any time. We borrow t,his colorful terminology from t2he Swedish VIA project [8].

Erumple 1. We have a set of 11 tasks all having period 1, computation time 0.1, and skip factor 10. All 11 tasks can be accommodated provided that, at every period of length 1, one task instance can be skipped.

Err.mmple 2. We have two tasks: tl has period 1, computation time 1 and skip factor 10; t z has period 1, computation time 0.05 and skip factor infinity. This system can't be scheduled because tl can't give time to t 2 frequently enough even though a naive calculation of utilization, taking skips into account, (0.9 + 0.05) is less than 1.

Emmple 3. We have two tasks: tl has period 1, computation time 1, and skip factor 10; t 2 has period 15, computation time 1 and skip factor infinitmy. This system can be scheduled because every period of t z overlaps at least one skippable task instance of t l . Note that the utilization here (0.9 + 1/15) is actually higher t,han in example 2 above.

div.head: Alternative Models
div.p: Our model captures the situation of periodic radar signals entering a system where capturing every other one makes sense. It also captures the video display problem where we are willing to skip an occasional frame but frame arrivals are periodic. We rejected the following possible models because we considered them to be too permissive. Since they allow more freedom to the scheduler than our current, model, however, our algorithms will work for t,hose models. *Stale Skips: If a task skips tJhe current, period while working on instance i, it, c:a,n complek i by the deadline of the following period and count that as a single skip. In our model, an instance which misses its period is not worth completing.

0 Early Release: If a t,ask instance is skipped, the following red task may be released before the end of the period. In our model, skipping a task instance has no effect on the release time of the next instance.
a Statistical Model: Another possible model is a stmatistical one which says that, at. least, some fraction of deadlines must, be met during every some basic period.

div.head: Feasibility With Skipping is NP-Hard
div.p: When the first task instrance of some task is released is it red or blue? For a task with skip factor s, which is its first blue instance? The first,, second or maybe only the s'th. If the first blue instance of any task is the s'th we say that the system is deeply red. Of course when a system is schedulable assuming it is deeply red it is also schedulable without this assumption. First, we study the question of how hard it is to determine the best schedule off-line in the general case that tasks may be blue when they enter.

div.p: In the previous section we studied the problem of checking the feasibility of a system. In this section we woiiltl like to present some on-line scheduling algorit,hms for such systems.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Like telemarketing solicitations and political speeches, repeated signals arriving to a controller contain a great deal of redundancy. It is therefore sometimes acceptable to skip some of these signals. The question is: what can one gain by skipping them? This paper has presented algorit,hms that can take advantage of skipped task instances to schedule even overloaded systems under a fairly conservative model (no two skips in a row and a task inst,ance that meets the current deadline must be the inst,ance of the current period). The paper has also shown that determining the best task instances to skip is NP-hard. Since the Skip-Over algorithms allow idle time, we can use all the standard tricks for fitting sporadic t,asks into that idle time, e.g., [17, 4, 101 and [2] for the Earliest-Deadline-First Algorithm scheduling. Flitlure t,lieoretical work includes:

1. In tbe fixed priority model, we must determine how best t,o m e idle time. For example, is there a good variant of Blue When Possible for that model? Or maybe one should give different priorit,ies to blue and red instances of a task, so that blue tasks will execut,e as long as they do not harm red tasks. (for example use the Dual Priority Scheme [ 3 ] )
2 . Find an algorithm to deal with tasks whose skip parameters change over time.

Exploiting allowable skips is a tantalizing possibility for syst,ems that experience overload. The two simple algorithns we discuss here are just the first of many that, wait, to be discovered and evaluated.
